did_you_know.text: Did you notice that the Torah does not simply write “127 years,” but separates the hundred, twenty, and seven? At the end of the verse it emphasizes again: “the years of Sarah’s life”—all her years together.
Hebron, also called Kiriath-arba here, lies in the hill country of southern Canaan. The ancient city still exists and is considered one of the oldest cities in the region.

The words “stranger and resident” describe someone who is not a native of the place but has lived there for a long time. Abraham asks that his status as a resident be recognized so he can purchase a burial place.

In ancient times, the city gate was not merely an opening in the wall; it was also a meeting place for public and legal matters. That is why the transaction takes place before “all who entered the gate of his city.”

The name “Cave of Machpelah” is probably connected with the Hebrew root כפ״ל, meaning “double” or “doubled.” The Sages offered several interpretations, including a double cave or a cave containing pairs of buried people.
In this period, a silver shekel was a unit of weight, not a coin like those we use today. The phrase “current with the merchant” indicates silver measured by a standard accepted in trade.

The transfer of ownership includes not only the cave, but also the field, its trees, and all its boundaries. This detailed description resembles a legal document and emphasizes that the purchase was public and official.
